news.Title: UBS names top European chip stocks to watch ahead of Q3 2026 earnings season
news.Content:
Investing.com -- UBS analyst Francois-Xavier Bouvignies maintains a constructive outlook on European semiconductor stocks heading into third-quarter 2026 earnings, favoring companies with clear market share gains and meaningful exposure to artificial intelligence demand. In a September 29 research note, the analyst highlighted semiconductor capital equipment makers as top picks, citing AI-driven capacity expansion supporting a robust multi-year growth outlook.

The investment bank raised its wafer-fab equipment forecast for 2026 through 2028, projecting total WFE reaching approximately $225 billion in 2027, up 43% year-over-year, with potential to climb toward $275 billion to $300 billion by 2028. UBS maintains above-consensus earnings estimates for most covered companies, with 2027-2028 forecasts more than 10% above consensus across the sector.

1. ASML Holding NV (AS:ASML) (Buy, €2,350 price target)

ASML remains UBS's top pick in the European chip sector. The analyst expects the company to guide fiscal 2027 revenue growth above 30% year-over-year when it reports third-quarter results on October 14. UBS anticipates management will update capacity targets for low NA and immersion systems to exceed 30% growth in both 2027 and 2028. Pricing represents the largest earnings lever, with UBS analysis suggesting 15% to 20% EPS upside to consensus by 2028. The firm's third-quarter revenue estimate of €12.1 billion sits 3% above consensus.

2. ASM International NV (AS:ASMI) (Buy, €1,325 price target)

ASM International ranks as UBS's second preferred name, with the analyst forecasting 36% revenue growth in fiscal 2027 versus consensus at 29%, followed by 33% growth in 2028 versus consensus at 19%. This translates to EPS estimates 10% above consensus in 2027 and 20% above in 2028. For third-quarter results due October 27, UBS expects management to highlight improving visibility supported by advanced logic, memory, and mature-node demand. The stock currently trades at 7.9 times 12-month forward EV-to-sales versus its 10-year average of 5.7 times.

3. STMicroelectronics NV (NYSE:STM) (Buy, €80 price target)

STMicroelectronics completes UBS's top three picks, with the analyst's 2027 EPS estimate approximately 20% above current consensus expectations. UBS forecasts silicon photonics revenues reaching roughly $2.0 billion in 2027 and $2.5 billion in 2028. Combined with AI power products, total datacenter revenues are estimated at approximately $2.5 billion in 2027, representing about 14% of group sales, rising to roughly $3.8 billion or 19% of group sales by 2028. For third-quarter results on October 29, UBS expects fourth-quarter revenue guidance up approximately 10% quarter-over-quarter, ahead of normal seasonality.

news.Title: Apple, Meta, and SpaceX Are Driving a Device Boom—These 3 Stocks Could Benefit
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in Qualcomm Incorporated? Here are five stocks we like better.

Qualcomm still collects royalties on nearly every smartphone sold, a high-margin cushion even as Apple designs more of its own silicon

STMicroelectronics supplies the alignment chip inside nearly all Starlink terminals, tying its growth to SpaceX satellite capacity

Oura is targeting a reported $15 billion valuation with 5 million paid members and 85% 12-month subscription retention

Three weeks, four launches. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) put its first foldable on sale, unveiling the iPhone Duo alongside the iPhone 18 Pro on Sept. 9. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) rolled out an entire lineup of AI glasses, plus a pocket device built around its Muse agent. SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) pushed its first batch of next-generation Starlink satellites into orbit. And a smart ring company started marketing shares to the public.

Consumer hardware has not had a stretch like this in years. The money that follows a new device rarely lands on the company whose logo is on the box, though. It lands on the supplier, the patent holder, or the subscription attached to the thing you wear.

→ AST SpaceMobile's New Securities Lawsuit Adds Fuel to an Already Volatile Stock

Behavior Change, Not Hype, Decides Which Device Stocks Work

Josh Baylin, editor of the True Innovations Report at Stansberry Research, runs every hardware cycle through the same filter. Early adopters buy first, mass adoption follows, and then behavior shifts permanently. That last step is where household spending gets reassigned.

He points to the iPod as the cleanest example. The device itself mattered less than what it killed. CD binders and disc changers disappeared, and the dollars that used to buy physical music got rerouted into streaming services that did not exist yet.

→ Akamai's Anthropic Deal Puts $5.5 Billion Behind Its Edge AI Pivot

Baylin sees AI running the same play on a compressed timeline, moving from developers to everyday users faster than PCs or smartphones did. His three names are positioned against that behavioral shift rather than against any single hit product.

Qualcomm's Royalty Stream Outlasts Any Single Design Win

Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM) has been the intellectual property backbone of cellular since 3G, and Baylin's case rests there. Even when a handset maker skips Qualcomm's chip, that phone generally still pays Qualcomm a royalty. It is high-margin revenue that scales with the total device count, not with market share in any one socket.

Story Continues

→ Why 3 Struggling Stocks Are Suddenly Spending Big on Buybacks

That cushion matters because the socket pressure is real. Management now expects its share of Apple's latest iPhone launch to come in materially lower than a prior estimate of 20%, and handset revenue fell 20% year over year in the most recent quarter.

The stock reflects that tension. Shares hit an all-time high near $260 in May before sliding roughly 35% into late July, and the five-year total return sits at 44%, against 77% for the S&P 500. Baylin's argument is that a domestic semiconductor supplier with auto, internet-of-things and early data center exposure gets re-rated if personal device counts multiply across wrists, ears and faces. Qualcomm's first hyperscaler data center deal sent shares up 15% when it was disclosed in April, which suggests the market will pay for that pivot if it shows up in revenue.

STMicroelectronics Sells the Antenna Chips Inside Every Starlink Dish

The second name is a supplier route into satellite broadband. STMicroelectronics (NYSE: STM) co-designs the radio-frequency front-end modules that make Starlink's phased-array antennas work, with hundreds of them in each terminal.

More than 5 billion of those chips have shipped to SpaceX over the past decade, and the executive running that business told Reuters volumes could double within two years. The company puts its low Earth orbit (LEO) revenue near $600 million annually and targets $3 billion by 2030.

That upgrade stopped being theoretical this week. Starship reached orbit for the first time on Sept. 28 and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, each built to move roughly 10 times the data of the satellites currently flying. More bandwidth per satellite means more terminals sold, and every terminal carries ST's chips.

Concentration is the obvious risk, and Baylin does not dodge it. His counterpoint is that no credible competitor to Starlink exists today, and that Viasat (NASDAQ: VSAT) carries more business-loss exposure than ST does. Competing constellations could also become customers, since Amazon.com (NASDAQ: AMZN) is building out its own LEO network and European operators are pursuing theirs.

Oura's IPO Puts a Software Multiple on a Piece of Jewelry

The third name is the newest. Oura (NASDAQ: OURA) opened its roadshow on Sept. 21, marketing 50 million shares at $40 to $44 for a fully diluted valuation near $15.6 billion, with pricing expected during the week of Sept. 28.

The attach and renewal rates are what turn Oura's $15.6 billion IPO into something other than a hardware story. The company served 5 million paid members as of June 30, double the prior year, with 12-month retention near 85% and $1.4 billion in trailing revenue. It moved 3.6 million rings in the year through June, and 94% of buyers convert to the paid membership.

There is a distribution wrinkle worth watching. Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ: HOOD) is an underwriter on the deal, its first such role, giving it direct influence over how many shares reach retail accounts. A device with an unusually loyal user base, sold partly through the app those users already hold, is a new kind of IPO mechanic.

Baylin's advice for anyone tempted is borrowed from Peter Lynch. If you use it, like it and keep renewing, owning it is defensible. The day you stop renewing is the day the membership math starts breaking, and the subscription is what the valuation rests on. Hardware still accounts for roughly 80% of revenue, so the recurring layer has to keep growing into that gap.

Watch renewals at Oura, royalty revenue at Qualcomm and terminal shipments at STMicroelectronics. Those three lines tell you whether the behavior change actually stuck.

news.Title: European equities give up gains despite oil decline and Anthropic’s outlook
news.Content:
Investing.com - European stock bourses reversed course on Tuesday, closing lower, as investors continued to digest a spike in global bond yields and oil volatility.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.1%. Germany's DAX was flat, while France's CAC 40 and London's FTSE 100 slipped around 0.5% each.

European semiconductor shares rose on reports that AI startup Anthropic's IPO prospectus pointed to a sharp increase in spending on cloud, computing and infrastructure.

X-Fab shares rose 6.5% in Paris, while ams OSRAM gained 5.9%. Technoprobe rose 6.3% in Milan.

In Germany, Infineon Technologies rose 3.1%, Aixtron gained 4% and Siltronic climbed 4.6%. Amsterdam-listed ASML Holding rose 3.2%, ASM International gained 3.8% and BE Semiconductor Industries rose 3%.

STMicroelectronics gained 2.6%, while Soitec rose 3.9%. In Vienna, AT&S gained 4.8%, while Brussels-listed Melexis rose 3.9%.

September losses snap six-month winning streak

Equities have gyrated erratically throughout the month, coming under severe pressure as sky-high sovereign yields touched their highest levels since the 2008 global financial crisis.

A combination of a fresh European Central Bank rate hike, persistent hawkish commentary from central bank policymakers, and sudden development slowdown warnings from artificial intelligence pioneers added fuel to the broad-based sell-off.

The STOXX 600 was down nearly 2% for the month - on track for its first monthly decline in six months.

"AI investment is becoming less about promising narratives and more about companies' ability to deliver on them," said Javier de Berenguer, Fund Selector at MAPFRE Asset Management.

Sovereign yields serve as a fundamental anchor for global financial markets. They act as the benchmark reference price for pricing riskier equities and set the baseline borrowing costs for corporate debt and mortgages.

As sovereign bond yields surge, the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings expands, compressing equity valuation multiples across continental trading desks.

Diplomatic fatigue and geopolitical stalemate

Adding to market exhaustion, the brief prospect of a diplomatic breakthrough in the Middle East flared and rapidly dissipated earlier in the month, leaving institutional trading desks deeply fatigued.

Story Continues

The market has effectively settled into a frustrating stalemate following a torrential exchange of harsh rhetoric between U.S. President Donald Trump and Iranian leadership over the Strait of Hormuz. With diplomacy stalled and military posture remaining tense, energy markets remain trapped in a elevated risk regime that prevents a broader relief rally across rate-sensitive equity sectors.

Equities have been held back to some extent by geopolitical risk, Berenguer added. "

"Increasing exposure to longer-term debt could be a sensible strategy."

Consumer confidence and ECB speeches in focus

On the economic calendar, market participants are eyeing euro zone consumer confidence data due later in the session for clues on household sentiment amid rising energy costs and elevated borrowing rates.

Attention will also center on upcoming remarks from ECB President Christine Lagarde. Traders will scan her comments for any indications of whether persistent energy market volatility could force the central bank to maintain its restrictive monetary policy stance for longer into the final quarter.

Among other stock moves, Eiffage shares fell 3.4%, while Vinci shares dropped 2.8% after the French government proposed a significant increase in the tax on motorway concessions and major airports.

Lindt & Sprüngli fell 7% after the Swiss chocolate maker cut its full-year organic sales growth forecast.

news.Title: Cirrus Logic Faces Pricing Pressure: Can Gross Margin Stay Firm?
news.Content:
Cirrus Logic, Inc. CRUS reported a non-GAAP gross margin of 52.7% for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, alongside non-GAAP gross profit of $242.1 million. The margin declined sequentially, primarily reflecting previously expected pricing reductions, although cost cuts partially offset the impact. Compared with the year-ago quarter, gross margin increased slightly, mainly due to a favorable product mix, partly offset by higher freight and supply-chain costs. The company also highlighted that anticipated pricing reductions partially offset year-over-year revenue growth.

For the second quarter of fiscal 2027, Cirrus Logic expects GAAP gross margin between 52% and 54%. On the last earnings call, management stated that the quarter should receive a temporary benefit from wafers purchased under prior agreements with GlobalFoundries at favorable pricing. However, this tranche of lower-cost wafers is expected to largely sell through during the fiscal second quarter, after which gross margin is expected to normalize.

During the earnings call, management reiterated its long-term gross-margin outlook despite ongoing discussion around input costs across the supply chain. The company noted that many of the costs currently flowing through its results had been agreed upon well in advance and were therefore coming through largely as expected. At the same time, the company continues to monitor input-cost developments closely. To address potential pressure, management said it will aggressively pursue cost reductions and consider targeted price increases where warranted.

Supply-chain conditions remain an important consideration. Cirrus recently entered into a new capacity reservation and wafer supply agreement with GlobalFoundries that secures dedicated wafer capacity and pricing for calendar years 2027 and 2028. In addition, the company highlighted that newly developed products for smart-meter and adjacent applications are expected to carry gross margins well above the corporate average, while also broadening its addressable market.

Overall, Cirrus is managing previously anticipated pricing reductions, higher freight and supply-chain costs and broader input-cost uncertainty while maintaining its long-term gross-margin outlook and guiding second-quarter gross margin to 52-54%.

Taking a Look at CRUS' Competitors

Qualcomm Incorporated QCOM faces mounting earnings risk as handset weakness, lower Apple modem share and rising input costs weigh on QCT profitability. Memory-driven demand pressure and customer mix shifts are constraining mobile, while price increases will take time to offset higher wafer, assembly, test and packaging costs. Data center expansion also carries execution risk because near-term custom silicon revenue is expected to dilute QCT gross margins before the platform reaches scale. Elevated spending on new compute programs and debt above cash and marketable securities further limit flexibility. Qualcomm's QCT EBT margin declined to 26% from 30% as higher product costs offset higher average selling prices. For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, the company expects QCT EBT margin of 23-25% and total revenue of $9.7-$10.5 billion.

Story Continues

Skyworks Solutions, Inc. SWKS is benefiting from sustained Broad Markets growth, led by Wi-Fi adoption, automotive connectivity and data center timing and power products. Rising RF complexity and a multi-generational Android win support the Mobile content outlook, while the Qorvo combination could add scale, diversification and cost savings. Near-term demand remains steady, and the fall smartphone ramp should lift Mobile revenue. For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Skyworks expects revenues to be between $1.01 billion and $1.06 billion. Mobile revenues are expected to grow sequentially in the high teens, driven by seasonal product launches at the largest customer. Broad Markets is projected to increase approximately 5% year over year and represent about 39% of sales. The company anticipates gross margin between 44% and 45%.

CRUS Price Performance, Valuation and Estimates

Shares of CRUS have lost 18% in the past three months compared with the Electronics-Semiconductors industry's decline of 12.4%.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

CRUS is trading at a forward 12-month price/earnings ratio of 15.98, higher than the Electronics-Semiconductors sector's multiple of 13.93.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for CRUS' earnings for fiscal 2027 has been revised downward over the past 60 days.

CRUS currently has a Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell).
